zh.q: 刺激神经的一端，电表指针会怎么动？
zh.concl: 兴奋是以电信号的形式沿着神经纤维传导的，这种电信号也叫神经冲动。
points: 静息时电表没有测出电位变化，说明神经表面各处电位相等。
刺激左端后，靠近刺激端的 a 处先变为负电位，接着恢复正电位。
随后另一电极 b 处变为负电位，接着又恢复为正电位。

zh.q: 没有刺激时，膜内外为什么是内负外正？
zh.concl: 静息时膜主要对 K⁺ 有通透性，K⁺ 外流使膜外阳离子浓度高于膜内，膜两侧表现为内负外正，这就是静息电位。
points: 细胞外的 Na⁺ 浓度比膜内高，K⁺ 浓度比膜内低。
静息时膜主要对 K⁺ 有通透性，造成 K⁺ 外流。
K⁺ 外流使膜外阳离子浓度高于膜内，膜两侧表现为内负外正，即静息电位。

zh.q: 给膜一个刺激，膜电位会怎样变？
zh.concl: 受刺激时膜对 Na⁺ 通透性增加、Na⁺ 内流，该部位出现内正外负的兴奋状态，此时的膜电位称为动作电位。
points: 受刺激时细胞膜对 Na⁺ 的通透性增加，Na⁺ 内流。
这个部位出现暂时性的电位变化，表现为内正外负的兴奋状态。
此时的膜电位称为动作电位；邻近未兴奋部位仍是内负外正。

zh.q: 兴奋是怎样沿神经纤维一段一段传下去的？
zh.concl: 兴奋部位与未兴奋部位之间的电位差形成局部电流；局部电流刺激相近的未兴奋部位兴奋，于是兴奋向前传导，后方恢复静息。
points: 兴奋部位与未兴奋部位之间存在电位差，电荷移动形成局部电流。
局部电流又刺激相近的未兴奋部位发生同样的电位变化。
如此进行下去，兴奋向前传导，后方又恢复为静息电位。

zh.q: 兴奋怎样跨过两个神经元之间的缝隙？
zh.concl: 突触由突触前膜、突触间隙与突触后膜构成；递质由突触小泡释放、扩散过间隙、与后膜受体结合，引发突触后膜电位变化。
points: 相邻的两个神经元并不是直接接触的。
突触由突触前膜、突触间隙与突触后膜构成；轴突末梢处有许多突触小泡。
递质由小泡释放、扩散过间隙、与后膜受体结合，引发后膜电位变化；随后被降解或回收。

zh.q: 为什么兴奋只能单向传，而且比在纤维上慢？
zh.concl: 递质只存在于突触小泡中、只能由突触前膜释放，所以神经元之间的传递只能是单方向的；突触处要经过化学信号转换（有延搁），传递速度比在神经纤维上慢。
points: 递质只存在于突触小泡中，只能由突触前膜释放，然后作用于突触后膜上。
因此神经元之间兴奋的传递只能是单方向的，例如从轴突传到下一个神经元的胞体或树突。
突触处要经过化学信号的转换（有延搁），单位距离上比在神经纤维上慢得多。

zh.q: 可卡因为什么让人上瘾？
zh.concl: 可卡因使突触前膜上的转运蛋白失去回收多巴胺的功能，多巴胺留在突触间隙持续发挥作用，导致突触后膜上的多巴胺受体减少；药效过后受体已减少，只能继续用药，形成恶性循环。
points: 这类物质对神经系统的影响，作用位点往往在突触。
正常时多巴胺发挥作用后，会被突触前膜上的转运蛋白回收。
可卡因使转运蛋白失去回收多巴胺的功能：多巴胺留在间隙持续发挥作用，导致后膜上的多巴胺受体减少（真实的受体减少是天到周的过程，界面压缩成几秒，示意）。

zh.q: 降低膜外 Na⁺ 浓度，动作电位会怎样变？
zh.concl: 改变轴突外 Na⁺ 浓度，静息电位并不受影响，但动作电位的幅度会随着 Na⁺ 浓度的降低而降低。
points: 改变轴突外 Na⁺ 浓度，静息电位并不受影响。
动作电位的幅度会随着 Na⁺ 浓度的降低而降低。
峰值的幅度跟着膜外与膜内 Na⁺ 的浓度差走，而静息电位由 K⁺ 外流决定（教材原文只说「随浓度降低而降低」，不要记成「正比」）。

zh.q: 考核：把动作电位恢复成正常
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：把膜外 Na⁺ 调回 100 %、保持刺激、解除阻断，动作电位就恢复成正常。
points: 峰值要回到 +28.9 mV 以上：膜外 Na⁺ 不能太低，通道也不能被阻断。
静息电位不受膜外 Na⁺ 影响，看它是不是 −70 mV 就知道膜片是否安静。
阻断 Na⁺ 通道就没有动作电位——这是麻药与毒素的作用方式。

en.q: Stimulate one end of the nerve. How will the meter needle move?
en.concl: Excitation is conducted along nerve fibers as an electrical signal, also called a nerve impulse.
points: At rest the meter detects no potential change, showing the nerve surface is at the same potential everywhere.
After stimulating the left end, point a near the stimulus first becomes negative, then returns to positive.
Then the other electrode at b becomes negative, then returns to positive.

en.q: Without a stimulus, why is the membrane negative inside and positive outside?
en.concl: At rest the membrane is mainly permeable to K⁺; K⁺ outflow makes the cation concentration outside higher than inside, so the membrane is negative inside and positive outside. This is the resting potential.
points: The Na⁺ concentration outside the cell is higher than inside, and the K⁺ concentration is lower.
At rest the membrane is mainly permeable to K⁺, so K⁺ flows out.
K⁺ outflow makes the cation concentration outside higher than inside, so the membrane is negative inside and positive outside: the resting potential.

en.q: Give the membrane a stimulus. How does the membrane potential change?
en.concl: When stimulated, the membrane becomes more permeable to Na⁺ and Na⁺ flows in; the region becomes excited, positive inside and negative outside, and this membrane potential is called the action potential.
points: When stimulated, the cell membrane becomes more permeable to Na⁺, and Na⁺ flows in.
This region shows a temporary potential change, an excited state that is positive inside and negative outside.
This membrane potential is called the action potential; neighboring unexcited regions are still negative inside and positive outside.

en.q: How is excitation passed down the nerve fiber section by section?
en.concl: The potential difference between excited and unexcited regions forms local currents, which stimulate nearby unexcited regions, so excitation is conducted forward and the region behind returns to rest.
points: There's a potential difference between excited and unexcited regions, and the moving charge forms local currents.
Local currents in turn stimulate nearby unexcited regions to undergo the same potential change.
And so on: the excitation is conducted forward, and the region behind returns to the resting potential.

en.q: How does excitation cross the gap between two neurons?
en.concl: A synapse consists of the presynaptic membrane, synaptic cleft and postsynaptic membrane; transmitter released from synaptic vesicles diffuses across the cleft and binds to postsynaptic receptors, changing the postsynaptic membrane potential.
points: Two neighboring neurons don't actually touch.
A synapse consists of the presynaptic membrane, synaptic cleft and postsynaptic membrane; the axon terminal holds many synaptic vesicles.
Transmitter is released from vesicles, diffuses across the cleft and binds to postsynaptic receptors, causing a potential change; it is then broken down or taken back up.

en.q: Why can excitation only cross in one direction, and more slowly than along a fiber?
en.concl: 递质只存在于突触小泡中、只能由突触前膜释放，所以神经元之间的传递只能是单方向的；突触处要经过化学信号转换（有延搁），传递速度比在神经纤维上慢。
points: Transmitter exists only in synaptic vesicles, can only be released by the presynaptic membrane, and then acts on the postsynaptic membrane.
因此神经元之间兴奋的传递只能是单方向的，例如从轴突传到下一个神经元的胞体或树突。
A synapse requires conversion to a chemical signal (with a delay), so per unit distance it's much slower than a nerve fiber.

en.concl: Cocaine stops the transporter proteins on the presynaptic membrane from taking dopamine back up, so dopamine stays in the synaptic cleft and keeps acting, which reduces dopamine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane; once the effect wears off the receptors are already fewer, so the user has to keep taking the drug, a vicious circle.
points: Substances like this usually act on the nervous system at the synapse.
Normally, after dopamine acts, it's taken back up by transporter proteins on the presynaptic membrane.

Cocaine stops the transporter proteins from taking dopamine back up: dopamine stays in the cleft and keeps acting, which reduces dopamine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane (the real loss of receptors takes days to weeks; it's compressed into seconds on screen, illustrative).

en.q: Lower the external Na⁺ concentration. How does the action potential change?
en.concl: Changing the Na⁺ concentration outside the axon doesn't affect the resting potential, but the action potential's amplitude falls as the Na⁺ concentration falls.
points: Changing the Na⁺ concentration outside the axon doesn't affect the resting potential.
The action potential's amplitude falls as the Na⁺ concentration falls.

The peak amplitude follows the Na⁺ concentration difference between outside and inside, while the resting potential is set by K⁺ outflow (the textbook only says "falls as the concentration falls"; don't remember it as "proportional").

en.q: Assessment: restore the action potential to normal
en.concl: The assessment has no new conclusion: set external Na⁺ back to 100 %, keep stimulating, remove the block, and the action potential returns to normal.
points: To get the peak back above +28.9 mV, external Na⁺ can't be too low and the channels can't be blocked.
The resting potential isn't affected by external Na⁺; check that it's −70 mV to know whether the membrane patch is quiet.
Block the Na⁺ channels and there's no action potential; that's how anesthetics and toxins act.
